a: the angel of repentance
t: The Shepherd begins the great parable
p: Similitude 9 is the longest part of the book. The Shepherd retells the tower of the Visions in a new form.
b: The angel of repentance first appeared to Hermas dressed as a shepherd in 25:1 (Vision 5.1), sent by the most revered angel to live with him (25:2). Since then he has given the twelve Mandates and eight Similitudes. Now he says he will show again what Hermas saw in the Visions, "more exactly" (78:3). So Similitude 9 is a second telling of the tower of Vision 3 (chapters 10-21), and it runs to 110, the longest unit in the whole book. Lake sums up the book's plan: "in the Similitudes the working and theological doctrine of repentance is developed." Who the Shepherd is, and who sent him, is set out in the note at 78:3.

a: For that Spirit is the Son of God.
t: "That Spirit is the Son of God"
p: The woman of the Visions was the Holy Spirit speaking, and the Shepherd says that Spirit is the Son of God.
b: The Greek is plain: ekeino gar to pneuma ho huios tou theou estin. Hermas speaks of "the Son of God," never "Jesus" or "Christ," in these chapters, and here he joins the Son and the Holy Spirit so closely that readers have struggled to say what he believed. John Chapman (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910) says "It has been thought with some reason that he did not distinguish the Son from the Holy Ghost," but that "his words are not clear." Lake's footnote on Michael at 69:3 (Similitude 8.3.3) says that this, with Similitude 9's Son, "makes it very hard to reconstruct the Christology of Hermas." Compare 59:5 (Similitude 5.6.5) and the Latin addition at 58:2. The capitals follow Lake's English; the Greek has none. Keeping them is the site's choice: the speaker is "the Holy Spirit" in the same sentence. Against it stands 8:1 (Vision 2.4.1), where the Church was "created first of all": Hermas does not say how the created Church and the Spirit who spoke in her form fit together.
orig: ἐκεῖνο γὰρ τὸ πνεῦμα ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν

a: when you were made strong through the Spirit
p: Lake prints "by the spirit" here and "the same Spirit" at the end of the verse. The site capitalizes both.
b: The Greek dia tou pneumatos has the article and no capital, like every word in the Greek. Lake's English writes "when you were strengthened by the spirit" with a small letter and then "yet through the same Spirit" with a capital; Crombie's English in the Ante-Nicene Fathers capitalizes both. The site follows Crombie here because the verse ends with "the same Spirit," which points back to this one and to the Holy Spirit of 78:1. This is a choice that touches doctrine: with a small letter, Hermas's own spirit, made strong, would be meant. "In your strength" is the Greek tē ischui sou.
orig: ἐνεδυναμώθης διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος καὶ ἴσχυσας τῇ ἰσχύϊ σου

a: as if a virgin were showing you
t: Why a virgin, then an angel?
p: Lake: the point is that the vision was fitted to what Hermas could bear, first in human form, then as an angel.
b: The Church first appeared to Hermas as an old woman who grew younger (Visions 1-4), and in 21:1 (Vision 3.13.1) she is young and beautiful. The Shepherd now says Hermas was too weak "in the flesh" to receive it from an angel, so it came through a woman. Lake's footnote: "The point is that the form of the vision was accommodated to Hermas' powers. It was at first sent in the form of a human being (the emphasis is on the humanity, not on the Virginity) and afterwards when he was stronger spiritually in the form of an angel." The word "virgin" (parthenos) also prepares for the twelve virgins of 79:3.

a: the glorious angel
t: Who sent the Shepherd, and who is he?
p: The glorious angel gave the Shepherd to Hermas. Hermas never says the Shepherd is the Son of God; the text keeps them apart.
b:
Three figures carry titles of honor. The Shepherd was sent by "the most revered angel" (25:2, Vision 5.2), here "the glorious angel." In 69:3 (Similitude 8.3.3) "the great and glorious angel" is Michael, and Lake's footnote there adds: "But in Sim. ix. he is the Son of God." And "the glorious man" who tests the tower "is the Son of God" (89:7-8). Hermas himself does not say whether the angel who gave him the Shepherd is the Son.

The Shepherd is "the angel of repentance" (78:1; Lake's introduction: "the shepherd, or angel of repentance"). In this part he is never the Son: the glorious man hands the rejected stones over to him (84:1), and he fears looking "careless in the master's eyes" (84:6). No source opened for this part argues that he is the Son or Michael. His last charge comes in Similitude 10 (111-114).

a: Arcadia
p: A mountain region of Greece, far from Rome. Lake: every witness has it, but it plays no further part.
b: Arcadia is a region of Greece. Hermas lives in Rome (1:1), so the trip is a vision journey, like the Spirit carrying him off in 1:3 (Vision 1.1.3). Lake's footnote: "Arcadia is found in all the authorities; but it plays no further part in the story. Zahn emends to Aricia; but Aricia is a village, and Monte Cavo, which might be intended, is not specially near to it." So the site keeps Arcadia, with Lake.

a: twelve mountains
p: Each mountain stands for a kind of believer. The Shepherd explains them in 94-106.
b: The Shepherd later says that the twelve mountains are twelve tribes living in the whole world, to whom the Son of God was preached by the apostles (94:1, Similitude 9.17.1). The tribes here are the nations of the world, not Israel's twelve tribes by birth. Each mountain's look (black, bare, thorny, half-dry, cracked, fruitful, white) matches the kind of people who come from it, and the next chapters (96-106) go through them one by one. The stones from the mountains are believers from all the nations; when the virgins carry them in, they all turn white (81:5).

a: thorns and thistles
p: The same pair of words as the Greek of Genesis 3:18 and Hebrews 6:8, land under a curse.
b: The Greek akanthai kai triboloi is the pair Hebrews uses of ground that "puts out thorns and thistles" and so "fails the test" (Hebrews 6:8), the same chapter that warns about those who fall away after being enlightened (Hebrews 6:4-6). The pair goes back to the curse on the ground: "Thorn and thistle it will sprout for you" (Genesis 3:18). Hermas does not quote either verse, but readers who knew them would hear a mountain under judgment. The Shepherd explains the third mountain at 97 (Similitude 9.20).

a: It was square, big enough to hold the whole world.
t: A square rock that holds the world
p: The rock is the Son of God (89:1). Its size fits what the Shepherd says in 91:5: he holds up the whole world.
b: "Square" (tetragōnos) is the shape of the good stones in both tellings of the tower (10:4, Vision 3.2.4; 80:3) and of the heavenly city: "The city lies in a square" (Revelation 21:16). The rock is higher than all the mountains and can "hold" (chōrēsai) the whole world. The explanation comes in 89:1-2 and 91:5: the rock is the Son of God, whose name "cannot be contained, and it holds up the whole world." The Greek plays on the words: the rock can hold the world, but the Son's name cannot itself be held (achōrētos).

a: That rock was old, and a gate had been cut into it
t: An old rock and a new gate
p: Hermas notices that the rock is old and the gate freshly cut. The Shepherd explains both in 89:1-3.
b: The puzzle is set up on purpose: old rock, new gate. In 89:2-3 the Shepherd answers that the Son of God is "older than all his creation," while the gate is new because "he appeared in the last days." Christian readers have long called Christ the rock ("that rock was the Christ," 1 Corinthians 10:4) and the way in ("I am the door," John 10:9, where the Greek word is thura, door, not Hermas's pulē, gate). Daniel's stone "cut from a mountain, though not by hands" (Daniel 2:45) is another rock cut out, though there the stone itself is cut, not a gate in it.

a: brighter than the sun
t: "Brighter than the sun" or "in the sun"?
p: The Greek huper ton hēlion means "beyond the sun." Lake's English has "glistened so in the sun."
b: The preposition huper with the accusative means "over, beyond, more than." So the gate shone more than the sun, like the light from heaven Paul saw on the road, "outshining the sun" (Acts 26:13). Lake translates "the door glistened so in the sun," taking the sun as the light it reflects. The Greek favors the stronger sense, and the site follows it.

a: Twelve virgins
p: Explained in 90:2 as holy spirits, powers of the Son of God, and named in 92:2 as virtues.
b: The Greek parthenoi means young unmarried women. Lake translates "maidens"; the site's Matthew 25:1 renders the same word "young women." Here the site keeps "virgins" because the Shepherd builds on the word (78:2) and on their purity. In Vision 3 seven women hold up the tower (16:2, Vision 3.8.2), and five of their names come back here: Faith, Self-control, Simplicity, Innocence and Love (16:7; 92:2). Lake's footnote on the arrangement: four at the corners and two between each pair, "so that the 'door' must have been a sort of porch, cut out of the rock, and the tower was built directly above it."

a: if you have any sense
p: The Greek sunetos ōn can mean "being sensible" (a warning) or "as if you were wise" (a rebuke).
b: The two words sunetos ōn, "being understanding," stand in the middle of the command. Lake punctuates them as advice: "be prudent, do not attempt them." Crombie's English in the Ante-Nicene Fathers takes them as irony: do not try to grasp them "as if you were wise." Either way the Shepherd's point is the same as Sirach's: "Do not go looking for things harder than you can handle" (Sirach 3:21), with the remedy added: ask the Lord, and receive sunesis. The site renders that noun "discernment," as in the name of one of the virgins (92:2), and keeps "understanding" for epistēmē (16:7).

a: six men
t: The six men and the crowd of builders
p: As in Vision 3, six tall figures direct the building. The Shepherd says they are glorious angels (89:8).
b: In the first telling, the tower was built "by the six young men who had come with her," while thousands of others brought stones (10:5, Vision 3.2.5). Here the six men summon the builders, and in 89:6-8 the Shepherd explains: the builders are "glorious angels," and the six are the glorious angels who stand at the right and left of the Son of God. The picture is of the church built by heaven's work, not by human hands alone. Revelation also sets angels at the gates of the city (Revelation 21:12).

a: a deep place
p: The first stones come up out of "the deep" (buthos). The Shepherd later says they came up through water.
b: In Vision 3 some stones came from the deep and some from the dry land (10:5, Vision 3.2.5), and the tower stood on water because the believers' life was saved, and will be saved, through water (11:5, Vision 3.3.5). Here the first hundred-odd stones rise from the deep and need no cutting. In 92:4 they are the righteous of past generations, prophets and apostles, and in 93:2 (Similitude 9.16.2) the Shepherd says they "had to come up through water" to be made alive: the water of baptism, which part 093-114 explains with "the seal."

a: loaded onto one another
t: How the virgins took up the stones
p: The virgins put the stones on one another, then carried them "one stone at a time" or "like a single stone": the Greek allows both.
b: The Greek epetithoun allēlais has a feminine "one another," so it is the virgins (feminine) who are loaded, not the stones (masculine): they set the stones on each other to carry. The next words, kata hena lithon ebastazon homou, are "they carried together, by one stone." Lake's English takes them as "carried them together like a single stone"; Crombie's has "each stone by itself." The site follows the second, because 81:1 then says how they carried each stone, the strongest at its corners.
orig: ἐπετίθουν ἀλλήλαις καὶ κατὰ ἕνα λίθον ἐβάσταζον ὁμοῦ

a: in the same formation in which they had stood
p: Lake's footnote: the four strongest kept to the corners and the others took the sides.
b: The Greek is compressed: "just as they had stood together around the gate, so the ones who seemed strong carried." Lake explains: "The meaning is that the four maidens kept to their original formation, with the four strongest at the corners, and the others in the middle of each side of the stone which they carried." The four at the corners are Faith, Self-control, Power and Patience (92:2): the strongest virtues bear the most weight.
orig: καθὼς δὲ ἐστάθησαν ὁμοῦ κύκλῳ τῆς πύλης

a: The rock and the gate were holding up the whole tower.
p: The church rests on the Son of God, the point the Shepherd draws out in 91:4-6.
b: In 91:6 the Shepherd says of the Son: "He himself became their foundation, and he gladly holds them up." Paul uses the same picture: "no one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:11). Ephesians puts apostles and prophets as the foundation with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Hermas has both: the stones from the deep (prophets and apostles, 92:4) are the foundation rows, but the rock and gate under them bear the whole building. In Vision 3 the tower was held up by seven women (16:2, Vision 3.8.2); here the rock bears it and the virgins carry the stones.

a: they all turned white alike
p: The stones from twelve different mountains lose their colors once the virgins carry them through the gate.
b: The change happens only to stones carried through the gate by the virgins (81:6, 81:8). The Shepherd explains it in 90:5 and 94:4 (Similitude 9.17.4): people from all nations, of every kind, become "one spirit, one body," and their clothes "all one color," once they receive the Son's name and put on these powers. White is the color of the twelfth, best mountain (78:10) and of the robes of the saved in Revelation (Revelation 7:9, 14).

a: they cannot change their colors
t: Only through the gate, only by the virgins
p: The builders may not set stones in themselves. A stone is changed only if the virgins carry it through the gate.
b: Two conditions run through the whole parable: the gate (the Son of God, 89:3-5) and the virgins (the holy powers, 90:2). Stones handed in without them stay as they were and are taken out again (81:6-7). The Shepherd later spells it out: no one enters the kingdom except through the Son's name (89:5), and the name alone is useless without the virgins' garment (90:2). So belonging to the church is not the same as being changed by it, a theme the explanation of the rejected stones develops (90:6-9).

a: there was a pause in the building
p: The work stops before the tower is finished. In 91:2 the Shepherd says why: time for repentance.
b: The Greek anochē means a holding back, a delay. Paul uses the word for God's forbearance: "in his forbearance God had passed over sins done earlier" (Romans 3:25; compare Romans 2:4). Hermas's answer comes in 91:2: "That is the very reason the building had a pause: so that if these people repent, they may go into the building of the tower." The same idea drives the whole book: the tower is not yet finished, and there is still time; in Vision 3 the end comes once the tower is finished (16:9, Vision 3.8.9; compare 13:5, Vision 3.5.5).

a: Sir
p: Hermas calls the Shepherd kurie, the same word Christians used for the Lord. Here it is a polite "sir."
b: The Greek kurie is the ordinary polite way to address a superior, "sir," and also the word for "Lord" used of God and Christ. Hermas uses it to the Shepherd in nearly every line of these chapters. The site renders it "sir" when Hermas speaks to the Shepherd and "Lord" when the text means God or the Son, as in 79:6 ("Ask the Lord") and 88:8 ("words of the Lord"). The tower's own "lord" (82:2; 84:1; 87:4) is the same word again, small here because it belongs to the story's picture; the Shepherd explains him in 89:8.

a: until its lord comes and tests this building
t: The lord comes to test the building
p: Like Paul's builders whose work "the fire itself will test," the stones wait for the lord's inspection.
b: The verb dokimazō, "test, prove," is the word for assaying metal and checking work. Paul uses it of the church's builders: "the fire itself will test what kind of work each one has done" (1 Corinthians 3:13). The lord's coming to his building also recalls Malachi: "all at once the Lord you are looking for will come to his temple" (Malachi 3:1). In Hermas the test happens in the vision (83:3-4), and the rotten stones it exposes are handed to the Shepherd to be cleaned and reworked, not destroyed (84:1-2).

a: the owner of the tower
p: Hermas uses three Greek words for the tower's owner. The site keeps one English word for each.
b: The figure who comes to inspect is called kurios, "lord" (82:2; 84:1; 87:4), authentēs, "owner" (here), and despotēs, "master" (82:7; 84:6; 86:4). The site gives each its own English word so the reader can follow the Greek. Authentēs, "one who acts on his own authority,"; its verb is the much-debated word in 1 Timothy 2:12. Here it simply means the one who has the say over the tower. In 89:8 the Shepherd reveals that this lord is the Son of God.

a: a man so tall that he stood higher than the tower
p: The Son of God appears taller than the tower, surrounded by six angels and many glorious beings.
b: Size shows rank. The six men were tall (80:1); this man stands higher than the whole tower, and the virgins run to kiss him (83:2). In 89:7-8 the Shepherd names him: "The glorious man is the Son of God." The church is great, but he is greater; it rests on him (the rock) and he alone judges which stones stay. The picture of a single great figure among angels at the judgment fits the Gospels' Son of Man who comes "along with the holy angels" (Mark 8:38).

a: All who had worked on the building were with him
t: Words Lake restored from the Latin and Ethiopic
p: The Athos manuscript lacks a phrase here. Lake's Greek puts it back from the Latin and the Ethiopic.
b: For this part of the book the only continuous Greek is the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s). Where it skips words, Lake translates the Latin versions (L) and the Ethiopic (E) back into Greek and marks it in a footnote: here "Retranslated from EL, om. A," placed after the words "all who had worked on the building." Lake's printed page marks where the restored words end, but not where they begin, so the exact extent of A's gap is not shown. See the variant. The sense is not affected: the builders and other glorious beings come with the lord of the tower.
orig: καὶ πάντες οἱ εἰς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν ἐργασάμενοι

a: some scabby, some cracked, some chipped
p: Black, scabby, cracked, chipped, neither white nor black, rough, stained: each stands for a kind of believer.
b: The seven defects are words for stone and skin. "Scabby" (epsōriakotes) comes from psōra, an itching skin disease, so the stone looks crusted. "Chipped" (koloboi) means docked or cut short; Lake translates "short." In 85 the Shepherd sorts them, and the explanations of the twelve mountains (96-106) show what kind of people each defect means: the chipped stones, for example, are "deceitful people and slanderers," cut short in their faith (103:7-8, Similitude 9.26.7-8).

a: some round ones too
p: Bright but round, they cannot be set in until they are cut square. In 107 they are the rich.
b: In the explanation (107:4-5, Similitude 9.30.4-5, which survives only in Latin) the round stones come from the white mountain: their "riches" (divitiae) had darkened them a little from the truth, though they never left God. So the Lord ordered their wealth to be "cut back" (circumcidi), not all of it, so that they could still do good with what was left, and they were set into the tower. The picture of stones too round to fit until trimmed is Hermas's version of the Gospels' warning about the rich and the kingdom (Mark 10:25). See also the elm and the vine (51, Similitude 2).

a: the glorious man, the lord of the whole tower
t: The lord hands the stones to the Shepherd
p: The Son of God, the tower's lord, gives the rejected stones to the angel of repentance to clean.
b: The order of the story matters for the book's message. The lord tests the building and finds rotten stones (83:4), but he does not destroy them. He hands them to the Shepherd, the angel of repentance, to clean and fit back in where possible (84:2). This is the book's teaching about sin after baptism in picture form: those who fell can still be reworked, through repentance, before the tower is finished (91:2). Compare 69:5 (Similitude 8.3.5), where Michael leaves those who broke the law to the Shepherd's authority for repentance.

a: when they have been rejected
p: The Greek word is the one used of the stone the builders rejected (1 Peter 2:4, 7), but here rejected stones can be reworked.
b: Hermas's word apodedokimasmenoi is the verb of Psalm 118:22 in Greek, quoted in 1 Peter 2:7: "the stone that the builders threw out, this one has become the head of the corner" (1 Peter 2:7). In 1 Peter the rejected stone is Christ. Hermas turns the word to the believers whom the lord has rejected from the tower (89:7): even these can be cut and set back in. The parallel is in the word, not a quotation.

a: the master may come suddenly
t: The master who comes without warning
p: The Shepherd works like the slave in Jesus' parables who must be ready when his master arrives.
b: The Gospel parables warn that the master "might arrive without warning and find you sleeping" (Mark 13:36), and that the careless slave's master "will show up on a day he is not looking for him" (Matthew 24:50). Here the angel himself is the servant who does not want to look "careless in the master's eyes." The urgency is the same as in 91:2: the tower will be finished, and the time for repentance is limited.

a: set them in the middle of the building
p: Weaker reworked stones go inside; sound ones go on the outside to hold the others.
b: The Shepherd had said so in 84:5: small stones in the middle, larger on the outside, "and they will hold the others together." The scabby, chipped and rough stones that could be cut go in the middle "because they were weaker" (85:4, 85:6); the cracked, half-white and stained stones that proved sound go outside. Lake's footnote on "weaker" (85:4): "i.e. to endure the strain of the outside." The church protects the weak by placing the strong around them (compare Romans 15:1).

a: twelve women
p: Beautiful, dressed in black, hair loose, they carry away the rejected stones. In 92:3 they are vices.
b: They mirror the virgins: twelve, with four stronger (92:3); belted with bare shoulders like the virgins (79:4), but in black instead of linen, and with their hair hanging loose. In 90:8 the Shepherd explains that these women seduced believers away from the virgins. Here they carry the rejected stones back to the mountains "cheerfully" (86:6): those who chose the vices are handed over to them (90:9). Lake's footnote marks words in this verse "Retranslated from LE, om. A": the Athos manuscript lacks them, and Lake puts them back from the Latin and the Ethiopic. His mark stands after "their hair hanging loose," and he does not mark where the words begin (see the variant).

a: savage
p: The Greek agrios means wild or fierce, the word for wild animals. Lake translates "cruel."
b: Agrios is used of wild animals and untamed land: John the Baptist ate "wild" honey (Mark 1:6). The women are beautiful ("very beautiful in form") and yet wild, which is the point of the picture: vice is attractive but untamed. The same mix returns in 90:8, where believers "desired" them for their beauty.

a: It seemed to me to be one solid stone.
p: The finished tower has no joints, as if carved from the rock itself. The Shepherd explains it in 90:5.
b: The Greek monolithos, "one-stone," is our word "monolith." A tower of many stones that looks like one carved from the rock is a picture of unity: "That is why you see that the tower has become one single stone with the rock" (90:5), because believers become "one spirit, one body." Vision 3 says the same of the first tower: its joints could not be seen, and it looked as if built from one stone (10:6, Vision 3.2.6).

a: the marks left by the stones
p: Lake: the holes left in the ground where stones were taken out are filled and leveled.
b: Hermas brings lime (asbestos) and fine ostrakon, which Abbott-Smith's lexicon gives as "an earthen vessel or potsherd": so fine bits of fired pottery. Lake's English has "a light clay" and Crombie's "fine-baked clay." Lake's footnote: "Apparently the meaning is that the holes left in the ground where stones had been taken out were to be filled up and levelled." The tower's surroundings must be clean and even before its lord comes (84:6; 87:4), and in 87:3 the virgins sweep away the kopria, which the same lexicon gives as "dung." Hermas helps with the work as the angel's assistant (87:2).

a: I grabbed his bag
p: The Shepherd first came with a bag on his shoulders and a staff (25:1). Hermas grabs it to keep him from leaving.
b: When the Shepherd first appeared he wore a white goatskin and carried a bag on his shoulders and a staff in his hand (25:1, Vision 5.1). The pēra is a traveler's or shepherd's bag, the one Jesus told the Twelve not to take: "no bag for the road" (Matthew 10:10). Hermas holds on to it and "adjures" him (horkizō, to put someone under oath) by the Lord. The scene is human and a little comic, as Hermas often is.

a: as a brother and not as a husband
p: The scene is chaste. The virgins call Hermas their brother, and the night is spent in prayer.
b: The text guards itself at every step: "as a brother and not as a husband" (88:3); Hermas is "ashamed" (88:3) and "silent" (88:5); the virgins "did nothing at all except pray" (88:7); asked what he ate, Hermas says, "I supped on words of the Lord all night" (88:8). Since the virgins are holy spirits and the virtues (90:2; 92:2), the story shows Hermas living among the virtues the Shepherd is about to name: they "are going to live with" him (88:3). Hermas's first sin in 1:1-8 (Vision 1.1) was a desire of the heart; here he sleeps among the virgins without one.

a: It was as if I had become young again
t: Claude's theory: the virgins act out the explanation
p: Claude's theory: the night scene acts out what 90:2-5 and 91:3 explain: clothed by the virgins, Hermas is renewed.
b: This is Claude's reading, not a published one that was checked. Two details line up with the explanation that follows. First, the virgins "spread their linen tunics" and lay Hermas in the middle (88:7), and in 90:2 a person enters the kingdom only if "these clothe him in their garment." Second, Hermas becomes "young again" (88:5), and in 91:3 he thanks God who "renewed our spirit ... and made our life new." In Vision 3 the Church grew younger as believers' spirits were renewed (20:2-3, Vision 3.12.2-3). If this is right, the night is a small acted parable of being clothed in the virtues and made young. It rests only on these verses.

a: I supped on words of the Lord all night
p: Hermas's answer echoes the Bible's picture of God's word as food.
b: The Shepherd asks a host's question, "What did you have for supper?" Hermas answers with a picture the Bible knows well: "People do not live by bread alone. People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth" (Deuteronomy 8:3), the verse Jesus quotes in Matthew 4:4, and Jeremiah's "Your words were found, and I ate them" (Jeremiah 15:16). The virgins have fed their guest the only food fit for them.

a: This rock and the gate
p: Rock and gate are both the Son of God: the ground of the church and the only way into it.
b: The Shepherd answers one question for two pictures: "This rock and the gate are the Son of God." The rock is what the tower stands on (81:2; 91:4-6); the gate is how stones get in (89:3-6). So the Son of God is both the ground of the church and the only way into it. Christian writers before and after Hermas used both pictures of Christ: the rock (1 Corinthians 10:4) and the way in (John 10:9; John 14:6). The chapter page of 89 sets out how readers take Hermas's Son of God, with Claude's own suggestion about the two pictures in a labeled box.
orig: ἡ πέτρα ... καὶ ἡ πύλη ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστί

a: older than all his creation
t: Older than creation, the Father's counselor
p: The Son existed before creation. J. B. Lightfoot: no Ebionite could have said this.
b: This verse is the plainest sign in Hermas that the Son existed before the world. J. B. Lightfoot (Galatians, 1874 printing, pp. 324-325), arguing that Hermas was "certainly no Ebionite" (the Ebionites held that Jesus was only a man), cites this verse and 91:5: Hermas "asserts that the 'Son of God was present with His Father in counsel at the founding of creation,' and holds that the world is 'sustained by Him.' Such expressions no Ebionite could have used." Lake's margin points to Proverbs 8:27-30, where Wisdom says "I was at his side, a craftsman" (Proverbs 8:30). In 58:3 (Similitude 5.5.3) the Lord's friends and counselors are the holy angels created first; here the Son alone is called the counselor.
orig: πάσης τῆς κτίσεως αὐτοῦ προγενέστερός ἐστιν
r: Proverbs 8:27-30; Wisdom of Solomon 9:9; Colossians 1:15-17; John 1:3; 58:3; 91:5

a: So he became the Father's counselor for his creation.
t: Counselor of creation, or to the Father of creation?
p: The Greek can be put together three ways. The site follows Lake's.
b: The Greek hōste sumboulon auton genesthai tō patri tēs ktiseōs autou can be construed three ways. (1) "Counselor of his creation" to the Father, as Lake's English: "he was the counsellor of his Creation to the Father." (2) Counselor to "the Father of his creation," taking the genitive with "Father." (3) A counselor with the Father in creating, as Crombie's English: "a fellow-councillor with the Father in His work of creation." The site follows the first. "His creation" can mean God's or the Son's own; the Greek does not say. Hōste with the infinitive gives a result, not a purpose, so the site writes "So he became," not "so that."
orig: ὥστε σύμβουλον αὐτὸν γενέσθαι τῷ πατρὶ τῆς κτίσεως αὐτοῦ

a: in the last days, at the completion of the age
t: He appeared at the end of the age
p: Lake: "the consummation," when this age is finished. The New Testament uses the same words of Christ's coming.
b: The Greek sunteleia is "completion, consummation." Lake's footnote: "The Greek means 'the consummation,' the time when this age or world-period is finished, and a new age will begin. (Cf. Mt. 13, 40.)" Hermas writes only "the last days of the completion"; the site adds "of the age" from Lake's note, as the site's Matthew 13:40 has "at the completion of the age." The verb phaneros egeneto is "became visible, appeared" (Lake "was manifested," Crombie "became manifest"), so the site writes "he appeared," not "he was made known": the Greek speaks of someone coming into view, not of news being told. Hebrews joins the same noun to the Son's appearing: "now, at the completion of the ages, he has been revealed once" (Hebrews 9:26), and 1 Peter says Christ "has been brought into the open in the last of the times" (1 Peter 1:20). An appearing fits a Son who already existed (89:2) and then came into view.
orig: ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τῆς συντελείας φανερὸς ἐγένετο

a: may enter the kingdom of God through it
t: Entering the kingdom through the gate
p: Lake's margin points to John 3:5 and the Gospel sayings about entering the kingdom.
b: Lake's margin cites John 3:5, Mark 9:47 and 10:23-25, and Matthew 5:20, 7:21 and 18:3, all sayings about who will "enter the kingdom." The site's John 3:5: "unless someone is born from water and Spirit, he has no way to enter the kingdom of God." The gate also recalls "Go in by the narrow gate" (Matthew 7:13), where the Greek word is Hermas's pulē, and Psalm 118:20, "This is the gate that belongs to the LORD; through it the righteous will enter."
r: John 3:5; Mark 9:47; Mark 10:23-25; Matthew 5:20; Matthew 7:13; Matthew 7:21; Matthew 18:3; Psalm 118:20

a: no one will enter the kingdom of God
p: To "receive the name" of the Son is Hermas's way of speaking of baptism, the seal (93:3-5).
b: Hermas repeats the phrase through these chapters: receive the name (89:4, 89:8), bear the name (90:2-3; 91:5-6). In 93:3-4 (Similitude 9.16.3-4) he says that before a person bears the name of the Son of God he is dead, but when he receives the seal he lays deadness aside, and that the seal is the water. So receiving the name is baptism into the Son's name (compare Acts 2:38; Acts 4:12, "no other name"). But 90:2 adds at once that the name alone does not save without the virgins' garment.

a: only one gate
t: A walled city with one gate
p: One way in: Hermas's picture of John 14:6, which Lake's margin cites at 89:6.
b: The New Jerusalem of Revelation has twelve gates, one for each tribe (Revelation 21:12). Hermas's city has one, because his point is that there is only one way in: "through the name of his Son, the one he loves." Lake's margin at 89:6 gives John 14:6: "Nobody comes to the Father unless he comes through me." "The one he loves" (tou ēgapēmenou) is close to Ephesians 1:6, "in the Beloved," and to the voice at Jesus' baptism, "This is my dearly loved Son" (Matthew 3:17).

a: These are the wall around the Lord.
t: The Lord walled in by angels
p: Lake: "here the Lord is for the moment identified with the tower."
b: The builders are angels, and "by these the Lord is walled around" (periteteichistai). Lake's footnote: "It is noteworthy that here the Lord is for the moment identified with the tower." The picture shifts: the city of 89:5, walled with one gate, becomes the Lord himself, surrounded by his angels, and the gate is the Son, "the one way in to the Lord." Hermas lets his images move without worrying about consistency, as apocalypses often do.

a: This is the one way in to the Lord.
p: Lake's margin: John 14:6.
b: Lake's margin sets John 14:6 here: "I am the way, the truth and the life. Nobody comes to the Father unless he comes through me" (John 14:6). Peter says the same of the name: "there is no salvation in anyone else" (Acts 4:12). Even the angels who build the tower come to God only through the Son (89:8).

a: The glorious man
t: Is Hermas's Son of God an angel?
p: The Son walks among six angels. Readers ask whether Hermas pictures him as the chief angel or above all angels.
b: Two lines in the text pull against each other. On one side, the Son of God appears as a "man" among six angels, only taller, and Hermas uses for him the word "glorious" he also uses for Michael, the great and glorious angel of 69:3 (Similitude 8.3.3). Lake's footnote there, on Michael: "But in Sim. ix. he is the Son of God," which together with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit "makes it very hard to reconstruct the Christology of Hermas." On the other side, this verse says that none of the glorious angels "will come in to God without him," and 89:2 makes the Son older than all creation, the Father's counselor. Lightfoot reads Hermas as holding a pre-existent Son (see 89:2); Chapman thinks his ideas "rather misty and confused than definitely erroneous." No source opened for this page argues that Hermas made the Son an angel; the chapter page sets out what the sources do say.
orig: ὁ ἔνδοξος ἀνὴρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστι

a: This tower," he said, "is the church."
p: Vision 3 and Similitude 9 tell the tower twice. Here are the main parallels and differences.
b: In Vision 3 the old woman tells Hermas that the tower he sees being built is herself, the Church (11:3, Vision 3.3.3). Both tellings agree: the tower is the church; it is built by six figures and many helpers (10:5; 80:1); some stones come from the deep and some from the land or the mountains (10:5; 80:3; 81:4); square, bright stones fit, others are rejected; women stand around it (seven in 16:2, twelve here); the building goes on so that sinners may repent before it is finished (13:5, Vision 3.5.5; 16:9, Vision 3.8.9; 91:2). Differences: in Vision 3 the tower stands on water (11:5), here on the rock and gate, the Son of God (89:1); in Vision 3 the Church herself explains, here the angel; and here the tower's lord comes to test the stones. The New Testament also pictures the church as a building: "you are being built up, as stones that live, into a spiritual house" (1 Peter 2:5; compare Ephesians 2:20-22).

a: They are holy spirits
t: Holy spirits, powers of the Son
p: The virgins are "holy spirits" and "powers of the Son of God": the virtues by which he lives in believers.
b: Hermas calls the virgins hagia pneumata, "holy spirits," plural and with no article, so the site writes it small. They are also "powers (dunameis) of the Son of God," and their names are virtues (92:2). Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Revelation speaks of "the seven Spirits in front of his throne" (Revelation 1:4). Hermas's twelve are the Son's own powers given to believers, so that the Son "himself bears the names of these virgins" (90:3). How the many holy spirits relate to the one Holy Spirit of 78:1 he does not say.
orig: ἅγια πνεύματα ... δυνάμεις εἰσὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ

a: clothe him in their garment
p: To be clothed with virtues is a New Testament picture too: "put on love."
b: Paul uses clothing for both baptism and the Christian life: "Every one of you who was baptized into Christ has put Christ on" (Galatians 3:27); "put on tenderhearted compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience ... On top of all these, put on love" (Colossians 3:12, 14). Hermas makes the two steps distinct: the name is received (baptism, 93:3-4), but the garment, the virtues, must also be put on and kept. "If you receive only the name ... it will do you no good at all."

a: For the Son himself bears the names of these virgins.
p: The virtues are first the Son's own. Lake: "The explanation is given in Sim. ix. 15" (92).
b: The names are the clothing, and the Son wears them first. Lake's footnote points ahead to 92 (Similitude 9.15), where the names are given: Faith, Self-control, Power, Patience, Simplicity, Innocence, Purity, Cheerfulness, Truth, Discernment, Harmony, Love. A believer who bears the Son's name must bear these too, because they are his character. The idea is close to Paul's "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 13:14).

a: have put on the power of these virgins
p: The Athos manuscript lacks words in this verse. Lake retranslates them from the Latin and Ethiopic.
b: Lake's footnote on this verse reads "Retranslated from LE, om. A": the only continuous Greek manuscript (A) lacks words here, and Lake puts them back in Greek from the Latin (L) and Ethiopic (E). His page does not show where the restored words begin. The meaning is clear from 90:2-3: the stones that stayed are those who put on the virgins' power.
orig: τούτων τῶν παρθένων τὴν δύναμιν ἐνδεδυμένοι εἰσί

a: one spirit, one body
p: Lake's margin: Ephesians 4:4, "There is one body and one Spirit."
b: The site's Ephesians 4:4 reads "There is one body and one Spirit" (Ephesians 4:4), with a capital, because Paul means the Holy Spirit. Hermas's "one spirit" here is the shared spirit of believers who have put on the many holy spirits (90:2), so the site writes it small; the echo of Paul's words is plain all the same. The tower that looks like one stone with the rock (86:7) is the picture: many believers, one body, "all one color" (81:5).

a: they thought the same things and did what was right
p: Lake's margin gives Paul's "think the same way" and the Bible's "does what is right."
b: "They thought the same things" (ta auta ephronoun) is Paul's phrase: "think the same way" (Philippians 2:2; 2 Corinthians 13:11), and Lake also cites Philippians 3:16, 4:2 and Romans 12:16. "Did what was right" (dikaiosunēn eirgazonto) recalls Psalm 15:2, "does what is right" (Lake cites it by the Greek number, Psalm 14:2), Acts 10:35 and Hebrews 11:33. These were real believers, strong and united, before they fell (90:8).
orig: τὰ γὰρ αὐτὰ ἐφρόνουν καὶ δικαιοσύνην εἰργάζοντο
r: Philippians 2:2; 2 Corinthians 13:11; Romans 12:16; Psalm 15:2; Acts 10:35; Hebrews 11:33; 90:8

a: they were talked into it by the women
t: Seduced by the women in black
p: Believers fell not by force but by desire, like the young man of Proverbs 7.
b: The verb anapeithō means to win over by persuasion. Proverbs paints the same scene with the seductive woman: "She sways him with her much persuading" (Proverbs 7:21). The fall is described as a change of clothes: they "put on" the women's power and "took off" the virgins' garment and power. Grief and bad temper, which the Mandates warn about (34; 40-42), are among the women's names (92:3).

a: the house of God
p: Hermas uses "the house of God" for the tower, the church, as 1 Timothy 3:15 does.
b: "The household of God. That household is the church of the living God" (1 Timothy 3:15); "that house is us" (Hebrews 3:6). Hermas moves easily between tower, building and house. To be "thrown out of the house of God" is to lose one's place in the church, and the next chapter asks whether such people can come back (91:1-2).

a: That is the very reason the building had a pause
t: A second chance for the fallen
p: Those who left the virgins can return if they repent before the tower is finished. Otherwise others take their place.
b: This is the book's central message in the parable's terms. Lake's introduction: "for sin after baptism there was still the possibility of forgiveness for those who repented, though this repentance would not avail more than once." The fallen stones here had received the name and the virgins' power (90:7) and then gave them up; still, "they will enter" if they repent. The limit is time, not the sin: once the tower is complete, those who have not repented "will be thrown out for good." Readers compare Hebrews 6:4-6, which says it is "impossible" to bring back to repentance those who fell away. The one repentance is set out in 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6), where the site discusses how the churches have read it.

a: all who are called by his name
t: "Called by his name" or "who call on his name"?
p: The Greek can mean either. Lake translates "who call upon his name," but his margin cites Isaiah 43:7.
b: The participle epikaloumenois with the dative tō onomati autou can be middle, "who call on his name" (Lake), or passive, "who are called by his name," that is, who bear it. Lake's margin cites Isaiah 43:7, which in the site's wording is "all who bear my name" (Isaiah 43:7). The passive fits the chapter, where believers are those who "bear the name" (90:2-3; 91:5-6), and James speaks of "the good name that was pronounced over you" (James 2:7). The site follows the passive and gives Lake's reading here.

a: he renewed our spirit
p: Hermas counts himself among the sinners the angel of repentance was sent to, and gives thanks.
b: The prayer turns from "they" to "us." Hermas has been told since Vision 1 that he and his household sinned (1:8; 3:1, Vision 1.3.1), and here he thanks the Lord for sending the angel of repentance "to us who had sinned against him." The words "renewed our spirit" repeat Vision 3, where the Lord "renewed your spirits" and the Church grew younger (20:3, Vision 3.12.3). "Already ruined" (katephtharmenōn) is a strong word for life wrecked by sin.

a: It cannot be contained, and it holds up the whole world.
t: The name that holds up the world
p: The Son's name upholds all creation, as Hebrews 1:3 and Colossians 1:17 say of Christ.
b: "He carries all things along by his word of power" (Hebrews 1:3); "all things hold together in him" (Colossians 1:17). Hermas says it of the Son's name: it "holds up" (bastazei) the whole world, the same verb used for the virgins carrying stones (79:4) and for the rock carrying the tower (81:2). Lake translates achōrētos "incomprehensible," but its first sense is "that cannot be held," which plays on the rock that could "hold the whole world" (79:1). Lightfoot cites this verse, with 89:2, as a sign that Hermas was no Ebionite.
orig: ἀχώρητον καὶ τὸν κόσμον ὅλον βαστάζει

a: because they are not ashamed to bear his name
p: The Son carries those who are not ashamed of him, as in Mark 8:38 and Romans 1:16.
b: Jesus warns, "Suppose anyone is ashamed of me and my words ... Then the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person too" (Mark 8:38), and Paul says, "I am not ashamed of the good news" (Romans 1:16). Hermas himself ties the name to suffering: in Vision 3 "the right side of the holy place" belongs to those who suffered "for the sake of the Name" (10:1, Vision 3.2.1).

a: Faith
t: The names of the twelve virgins
p: Four strong virtues at the corners and eight between. The site keeps one English word for each Greek name.
b: The Greek names: Pistis Faith, Enkrateia Self-control, Dunamis Power, Makrothumia Patience; then Haplotēs Simplicity (single-heartedness), Akakia Innocence, Hagneia Purity, Hilarotēs Cheerfulness, Alētheia Truth, Sunesis Discernment, Homonoia Harmony, Agapē Love. Lake's English has Temperance, Long-suffering, Guilelessness, Holiness, Joyfulness and Concord for some of them. Faith comes first and Love last, as in the seven women of Vision 3, where Faith gives birth to Self-control and the chain ends in Love (16:7, Vision 3.8.7). Paul's list of the Spirit's fruit shares four of them: love, patience, faithfulness, self-control (Galatians 5:22-23); so does 2 Peter 1:5-7, which also begins with faith and ends with love. Vision 3's Epistēmē (16:7) is a different Greek word: the site renders it "Understanding" and Sunesis "Discernment," as its Baruch 3:9-4:4 entry does, so the two stay apart (compare "receive discernment" in 79:6).
orig: Πίστις, Ἐγκράτεια, Δύναμις, Μακροθυμία· Ἁπλότης, Ἀκακία, Ἁγνεία, Ἱλαρότης, Ἀλήθεια, Σύνεσις, Ὁμόνοια, Ἀγάπη

a: Unbelief
t: The names of the twelve women
p: Four stronger vices and eight followers, each the opposite of a virgin.
b: The Greek: Apistia Unbelief, Akrasia Lack of Self-control, Apeitheia Disobedience, Apatē Deceit; then Lupē Grief, Ponēria Wickedness, Aselgeia Shameless Living, Oxucholia Bad Temper, Pseudos Lying, Aphrosunē Foolishness, Katalalia Slander, Misos Hatred. The first three answer the first virgins directly: Unbelief against Faith, Lack of Self-control against Self-control. Several are subjects of whole Mandates: slander (27, Mandate 2), lying (28, Mandate 3), bad temper (33-34, Mandate 5), grief (40-42, Mandate 10). "Shameless living" is the site's word for aselgeia in Galatians 5:19.
orig: Ἀπιστία, Ἀκρασία, Ἀπείθεια, Ἀπάτη· Λύπη, Πονηρία, Ἀσέλγεια, Ὀξυχολία, Ψεῦδος, Ἀφροσύνη, Καταλαλιά, Μῖσος

a: will see the kingdom of God, but he will not enter it
p: Lake's margin: Deuteronomy 34:4, Moses sees the land but does not go in.
b: Lake's margin cites Deuteronomy 34:4, where the LORD tells Moses: "I have let you see it for yourself, but you will not go over there" (Deuteronomy 34:4). A "slave of God" who wears the vices' names is a real believer who has seen the kingdom and still stays outside. Compare John 3:3 and 3:5, where seeing and entering the kingdom stand side by side.

a: The forty are apostles and teachers
t: The four rows of the foundation
p: Ten, twenty-five, thirty-five and forty: the righteous of the first ages, the prophets, and the apostles.
b: The stones from the deep are the foundation rows: the first generation; the second generation of righteous people; "God's prophets and his servants"; and "apostles and teachers of the preaching of the Son of God." Paul lists "first, apostles; second, prophets; third, teachers" (1 Corinthians 12:28), and Ephesians 2:20 builds the church "on the apostles and prophets as the foundation." Hermas gives no names or dates for the first two rows. Claude's inference, not his words: since God's prophets come third and the apostles of the Son fourth, the two "generations" seem to be the righteous of still earlier times. The numbers have puzzled readers. Lake's footnote: "It must be noted that the numbers given here do not quite agree with those in Sim. ix. 4, and no satisfactory hypothesis has ever been suggested as to any hidden meaning which the numbers may conceal" (81:3 and 82:4 have twenty, not twenty-five). "His servants" (diakonoi) here is not the church office of deacon but God's ministers alongside the prophets.

a: until they fell asleep
p: "Falling asleep" is the early Christian way to speak of a believer's death.
b: The Greek koimēsis, "falling asleep," became the usual Christian word for death, the word behind "cemetery" (a sleeping place). Paul writes "about those who are falling asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The next chapter (93:5, Similitude 9.16.5) says the apostles and teachers, "having fallen asleep," preached to those who had fallen asleep before them. Here the point is that the spirits never left these first believers, unlike the fallen stones of 90:8.
